advisories.title: Consent Phishing via Unrestricted OAuth Client Registration
advisories.summary:
### Summary

The OAuth dynamic client registration endpoint is unauthenticated and accepts any HTTPS redirect
URI, and the consent screen renders the attacker-supplied client name and logo without marking the
client unverified or showing where the authorization code will be delivered.

### Details

The registration route carries only a public rate limiter - no session guard, no token check, no
initial access token - and is advertised in the server's OAuth discovery document, so it does not
have to be guessed. The redirect-URI validator in the dynamic-registration service accepts any
`https:` URI as well as loopback, so an arbitrary attacker-controlled callback registers cleanly and
receives a unique client id. The consent component then presents `client_name` and the client logo
with no unverified-client warning and without displaying the redirect host, leaving the user nothing
to distinguish a hostile client from a legitimate one. Dynamic registration exists only in the
enterprise and cloud editions; the community edition's OAuth controller has no registration route. The consent screen now shows the host that receives the authorization code and marks every client not registered by an instance administrator as unverified, without its logo. Dynamic registration also refuses client names that begin with NocoDB, including look-alike spellings.

### Impact

An unauthenticated attacker can register an OAuth client that presents itself as a trusted
application and obtain an authorization code from a single consent click by a workspace owner. The
code exchanges for an access token and a refresh token, granting persistent access to read and write
the victim's tables and records, read webhook and automation configuration and the integration
endpoints it exposes, and enumerate workspaces, bases and collaborators. Exploitation requires the
victim to approve the consent screen, so the severity rests on how convincingly a hostile client can
impersonate a legitimate one.

### Credit

This issue was reported by Foysal.

advisories.title: NocoDB 0.300.0 before 2026.08.0 Unauthenticated OAuth Authorization Code Creation
advisories.summary: NocoDB 0.300.0 before 2026.08.0 contains a missing authentication vulnerability in the POST /api/v2/oauth/authorize handler that allows unauthenticated attackers to create OAuth authorization codes. Attackers can send anonymous requests with client_id, redirect_uri and approved=true to insert unbounded ownerless authorization code records, limited only by rate limiting.

advisories.title: Stored Cross-Site Scripting via OAuth Redirect URI
advisories.summary:
### Summary

OAuth client registration accepted a redirect URI with any URL scheme, including `javascript:`, and the authorization endpoint handed that stored value back to the browser as a navigation target. A payload planted on a client the attacker owned therefore executed in the NocoDB origin when a signed-in user reached the consent screen.

### Details

The create and update schemas in the OAuth module validated `redirect_uris` with a generic URL check that accepts opaque schemes such as `javascript:`, `data:` and `vbscript:`, and client registration was available to any authenticated account, including an organization-level Viewer. Four paths then consumed the value without a scheme check: the consent screen's deny handler built its redirect entirely client-side from the raw query parameter; the deny branch in `oauth-authorization.service.ts` built a redirect before any validation ran; the error handler in the same path reflected the rejected URI back after validation threw; and the consent screen's approve handler assigned the server's response to `window.location`. Because `oauth.controller.ts` did not match the requested redirect URI against the client's registered list before a redirect was constructed, both buttons on the consent screen navigated the victim's tab to the attacker's scheme.

### Impact

Same-origin script execution in the victim's NocoDB tab. An attacker registers a client carrying a `javascript:` redirect URI and sends a consent link to a signed-in user; whichever button that user presses, the payload runs in the NocoDB origin and can read the session token from `localStorage["nocodb-gui-v2"]`, then call authenticated APIs as the victim - including against an administrator, leading to account takeover. Registering the client requires an authenticated account of any role; the victim only has to open the link while signed in.

### Credit

This issue was reported by [@CyberKareem](https://github.com/CyberKareem) and independently by [@Akokonunes](https://github.com/Akokonunes).

advisories.title: User Enumeration via Sign-Up Endpoint
advisories.summary:
### Summary

The sign-up endpoint answered differently depending on whether an email address already had an account, letting an unauthenticated caller test addresses.

### Details

`signup` in `users.service.ts`, and its Enterprise override, rejected an address that already had an account with a message saying the user already exists. The Enterprise version also answered an address with a pending invitation with a message saying it had already been invited. On an instance with open signup, an unregistered address simply creates an account. With invite-only signup turned on, an unregistered address was refused by `registerNewUserIfAllowed` with a different message and no account was created, so the two answers told registered and unregistered addresses apart without leaving anything behind. Sign-up now gives one answer for every address that already has an account, registered or invited, and with invite-only signup on, registered and unregistered addresses receive the same answer.

### Impact

No authentication is required. An attacker could learn whether an email address has an account on the instance and, where the Enterprise sign-up is in use, whether it has a pending invitation. On instances with invite-only signup this needed no account to be created. No account data or credentials were exposed.

### Credit

This issue was reported by [@NinjaGPT](https://github.com/NinjaGPT).

advisories.title: User Enumeration via Sign-In Error Message
advisories.summary:
### Summary

The sign-in endpoint returned a distinct error for an invited account that had not finished signup, revealing to an unauthenticated caller that the address belonged to a pending invitee.

### Details

`validateUser` in `auth.service.ts` checked whether the account found for the submitted email had a password salt. Accounts created by an invitation can have none until the invitee finishes signup, and for those it raised an error telling the user to finish signing up from the invitation email, without comparing the password. Every other failed sign-in, including one for an unknown address, received the generic invalid-credentials answer from `local.strategy.ts`. Accounts created through Google sign-in have a salt and received the generic answer. Every failed sign-in, including one for an account without a password, now runs the same password comparison and receives the same message.

### Impact

No authentication is required. An attacker could learn whether an email address belongs to an invited user who has not finished signing up, which also confirms that the address has an account on the instance. No account data or credentials were exposed.

### Credit

This issue was reported by [@NinjaGPT](https://github.com/NinjaGPT).

advisories.title: Revoked OAuth Access Tokens Accepted as First-Party Sessions
advisories.summary:
### Summary

OAuth access tokens are signed with the same secret as first-party session tokens, and the session
strategy short-circuits on the OAuth marker claim and returns the payload unchanged. Presenting an
OAuth token through the session header therefore bypasses the revocation check, client-existence
check, route allowlist and scope enforcement that apply on the bearer path.

### Details

Every OAuth-specific control lives in the bearer strategy: the revocation lookup, the client-existence check, the route allowlist and `granted_resources` scoping. `GlobalGuard` attempted the JWT strategy first, and that strategy returned the payload as-is when the OAuth marker claim was present, with no database lookup, no blocked-account check and no `token_version` comparison. Routes carrying an `@Acl` decorator refused it, but routes without one were reachable, among them the current-user, profile update and sign-out routes and the storage upload routes. In the Enterprise build, the exchange in `short-lived-token.strategy.ts` that turns a single sign-on token into a session also accepted an OAuth access token, revoked or not, and issued a full session with a refresh token, and the socket handshake in `NocoSocket.ts` accepted it as well. The session strategy, the exchange and the socket handshake now refuse OAuth access tokens, and the socket handshake also checks the user's current token version.

### Impact

A revoked OAuth access token continues to authenticate as its user for the remainder of the token's
lifetime. A third-party integration or MCP client that holds, or has leaked, an access token retains
authenticated write access after the user explicitly revokes the grant, can modify the victim's
profile, and can force a global sign-out at will. The same path bypasses client deletion, the
`granted_resources` scope restrictions, and the password-change revocation introduced for
CVE-2026-53926. Any deployment using OAuth or MCP integrations is affected.

### Credit

This issue was reported by uu K.

advisories.title: Session Cookie Without Secure Flag via Client-Side Token Sync
advisories.summary:
### Summary

The Enterprise web app wrote the session token into a cookie from script without the Secure attribute, so on an https deployment the token could travel over plain HTTP.

### Details

The Enterprise copy of the frontend composable `useGlobal/index.ts`, which the official Docker image is built from, writes the session token into an `nc_token` cookie from script each time the token changes and when the app loads. The write sets no Secure attribute, and a cookie set from script cannot be HttpOnly. The cookie the server issues at sign-in is HttpOnly, and Secure on https sites, but whenever the browser held no server-issued cookie, for example after it expired or was cleared while the token stayed in local storage, the app recreated the cookie without either attribute. The backend accepts this cookie as a session credential (`jwt-strategy.provider.ts`). The Community Edition copy of the composable sets Secure on https. The Enterprise copy now sets Secure on https as well.

### Impact

No authentication is required, but the attacker needs a position on the victim's network that lets them observe or induce a plain-HTTP request to an instance served over https, at a time when the script-written cookie is present. They could capture the victim's session token and act as the victim until the token expires.

### Credit

This issue was reported by [@iaohkut-from-NightWolf-Team](https://github.com/iaohkut-from-NightWolf-Team).

advisories.title: OAuth Access Token Accepted as First-Party Session
advisories.summary:
### Summary

OAuth access tokens are signed with the same secret as first-party session tokens, so the session
strategy accepted an OAuth bearer token as a full interactive session.

### Details

Access tokens issued by the OAuth token service were signed with the instance's JWT secret. The session strategy validated any such token and returned the associated user, so a token issued for a narrow OAuth scope authenticated its holder on first-party endpoints as though it were a browser session. In the Enterprise build, the exchange in `short-lived-token.strategy.ts` that turns a single sign-on token into a session also accepted an OAuth access token and issued a full session with a refresh token, and the socket handshake in `NocoSocket.ts` accepted the same token. The session strategy, the exchange and the socket handshake now refuse OAuth access tokens, and the exchange accepts only tokens minted for single sign-on.

### Impact

A token obtained for a limited OAuth scope could be used against first-party APIs with the full
privileges of the granting user, bypassing the scope restrictions the consent flow presented.

### Credit

This issue was reported by [@hash3liZer](https://github.com/hash3liZer),
[@XlabAITeam](https://github.com/XlabAITeam), [@keenanwgn](https://github.com/keenanwgn),
[@liangjs](https://github.com/liangjs), [@A7um](https://github.com/A7um), and
[@eros938](https://github.com/eros938).

advisories.title: Account Takeover via Base Invitation Resend
advisories.summary:
### Summary

Resending a base invitation writes a fresh signup token onto the target account before any
authorization check, and the base member list returns that token to base creators, so a creator can
take over any other member's account - including the base owner's or a super admin's.

### Details

`baseUserInviteResend` resolves the caller-supplied global user id and immediately writes a new
`invite_token` and expiry onto that account, before it checks base membership, pending-invitation
state, whether the account already holds credentials, or the target's role. Because the write
precedes the email-plugin check, the token is committed even on deployments with no mail plugin
configured, where the call itself returns an error. The base-users controller then selects the full
member projection for creators as well as owners, and that projection retains `invite_token`, so the
attacker reads back the token they just caused to be minted. Signup accepts token equality as proof
of identity for an already-registered account and replaces `salt` and `password` without requiring
the existing credential. `baseUserInviteResend` is absent from the creator exclude lists in both
editions' ACLs, and the enterprise edition overrides only `userInvite`, so both editions are equally
affected. Resending now requires the target to be a member of the base, checks for an email plugin before writing anything, and replaces the token only on an account that already holds one. The base member list no longer returns invitation tokens.

### Impact

A user holding the base creator role in a single shared base can take over another member's global
NocoDB account, inheriting every base, workspace and organization permission resolved for that user.
Targeting a base owner, workspace owner or super admin therefore yields broad administrative,
data-export, membership and deletion authority across tenants the attacker was never invited to, and
the victim is locked out because their password has been replaced. No user interaction, race
condition or token guessing is involved; email authentication, which is the default, is the only
precondition.

### Credit

This issue was reported by Vivek R and Mufeed VH of Winfunc. It was independently reported by [@dylanzonix](https://github.com/dylanzonix) (Dylan McGuinness, Ambit Security).

advisories.title: Invitation Token Disclosure in Workspace Member List
advisories.summary:
### Summary

The workspace member list is available to workspace viewers and returns pending members' raw
invitation tokens alongside the role each invitation was issued for, allowing the lowest-privileged
member of a workspace to redeem a higher-privileged invitation.

### Details

The ACL grants `workspaceUserList` to the viewer role, the list query in `WorkspaceUser.ts` selects
`invite_token`, and the workspace-users service returns those rows without passing them through
`sanitiseUserObj` - the shared sanitiser that already classifies `invite_token` as confidential
alongside `password` and `salt`, so the project's own notion of a secret is bypassed rather than
absent. The invite path writes the same value to the workspace-user row and to `nc_users`, so the
token exposed by the roster is exactly the one signup validates, and signup checks only token
equality and expiry with no verification that the caller is the invited party. Unauthenticated
requests to the roster are correctly rejected. The community edition is affected; the enterprise
edition selects the column but never persists a value there, so its rosters return null. The member list now leaves out invitation tokens in both editions.

### Impact

An authenticated workspace viewer can read a pending invitation token from the member list and
redeem it at signup, claiming the account and the role that invitation carried. Where an unexpired
workspace-owner invitation exists, this is privilege escalation from the lowest workspace role to
the highest, together with disclosure of a secret the codebase already treats as sensitive. The
attacker must already be a member of the workspace, and an unexpired pending invitation for a higher
role must exist. The official Docker image was not affected.

### Credit

This issue was reported by [@doanmanhducz](https://github.com/doanmanhducz).

advisories.title: Password Reset Token Not Invalidated on Password Change
advisories.summary:
### Summary

Changing a password from within the application updated the stored credential but left any outstanding password-reset token on the user record, so a reset link issued earlier stayed usable afterwards.

### Details

The in-application password-change path in `users.service.ts` wrote the new salt and hash and rotated the session token version, but did not clear `reset_password_token` or `reset_password_expires`. The reset flow in the same service locates an account solely by that stored token value, so a link issued before the change still matched a live row and still authorized setting a new password for the remainder of the token's expiry window. Nothing else in the change path revoked the outstanding token either.

### Impact

Someone holding an unexpired reset link - typically obtained through earlier access to the account's mailbox - could set a password of their own after the legitimate owner had already changed theirs, regaining control of the account in exactly the situation where the owner was acting on a suspected compromise. No authentication is required beyond possession of the reset link.

### Credit

This issue was reported by [@kunalmhaske21212](https://github.com/kunalmhaske21212).

advisories.title: Webhook Credential Exposure via Plugin List Endpoint
advisories.summary:
### Summary

The webhook plugin listing endpoint returned every configured notification plugin's stored configuration, including plaintext Slack, Teams, Discord and Mattermost incoming-webhook URLs, to any workspace-level collaborator.

### Details

Notification and storage plugins are an instance-wide administrative resource: the plugin list, read, update and test operations in `plugins.controller.ts` are all declared at organization scope and resolve only through the super-admin wildcard grant. The webhook listing route was a second, independently wired read over the same plugin rows, returning them unredacted, but it was declared at workspace scope and granted to the workspace Creator role in `acl.ts` - so the authorization middleware never evaluated an organization role for it.

### Impact

An authenticated user holding the Creator role on any workspace could read every notification webhook URL configured on the instance in plaintext, with no organization role, super-admin privilege, or access to the bases those notifications belong to. Those URLs are bearer-token equivalents and can be replayed directly against the messaging provider, outside NocoDB entirely, to post arbitrary messages into the organization's real chat channels.

### Credit

This issue was reported by [@iaohkut-from-NightWolf-Team](https://github.com/iaohkut-from-NightWolf-Team).

advisories.title: Insecure Direct Object Reference via Attachment Field Paths
advisories.summary:
### Summary

The v2 data write path accepted any attachment object carrying a path without binding that path to the caller, the base, the table or the column, so an attacker could store another base's attachment path in their own row and have NocoDB issue a signed download URL for it.

### Details

For non-v3 attachment fields, `prepareNocoData` in `BaseModelSqlv2.ts` validated only that each attachment object carried a url or a path. The surrounding checks covered JSON shape, rejected data URLs and applied a length limit, but never verified that the supplied path corresponded to a file reference owned by the caller's base or by the caller. On read, `_convertAttachmentType` collects every attachment object holding a path or url and calls `PresignedUrl.signAttachment()` on each, and the explicit download endpoint in `attachments.service.ts` behaves the same way: it reads the caller's own row through the normal row-level authorization check, finds the attachment object stored there and signs it. Row-level authorization therefore succeeded against the attacker's own row while the temporary signed URL pointed at the victim's stored file, which the secure download handler then served. 2026.08.0 bound paths written to attachment cells to files the caller or the base holds; the download endpoint still signed a foreign path stored in a JSON field, and encoded or bucket-prefixed storage URLs still passed as external links, until 2026.10.0.

### Impact

With secure attachments enabled, an authenticated user able to write to an attachment field in any one base could obtain a signed temporary download URL for an attachment belonging to a different base or workspace, given its stored path - crossing the base boundary and defeating the non-public download behaviour that secure attachment mode is intended to provide. Direct access to the victim base and direct download of the victim row's attachment both returned forbidden. Requires an authenticated account with write access to an attachment column in a single base and knowledge of the victim attachment path.

### Credit

This issue was reported by [@Faze-up](https://github.com/Faze-up).

advisories.title: Server-Side Request Forgery via Integration Remote Fetch
advisories.summary:
### Summary

An internal API operation that performs remote fetches on behalf of integrations accepted a fully caller-controlled URL, method, headers, and body, performed the request from the NocoDB backend, and returned the response to the caller.

### Details

The operation is exposed through the internal base API in `IntegrationPost.operations.ts` and handled in `integrations.service.ts`, which passed the supplied URL straight to axios with no destination validation and no request-filtering agent. Nothing restricted the destination to known integration provider endpoints or rejected loopback, link-local, private, or metadata addresses after server-side DNS resolution or after a redirect. The handler returned the response body, status, and headers, and additionally echoed back the expanded request configuration, which could carry decrypted integration secrets. The operation was granted at the base Editor level. From 2026.08.0 internal targets were refused and the expanded configuration was no longer echoed, but a request could still carry an integration's decrypted secret to any external host until 2026.10.1, which sends integration secrets only to the AI provider's own host, in its authentication header, and refuses placeholders of other integrations.

### Impact

Any authenticated user holding the Editor role on a single base - including one the attacker created themselves - could use the NocoDB backend as an HTTP client against services reachable only from the deployment network, such as internal APIs, services bound to loopback, administrative interfaces, and cloud metadata credential endpoints. Because the response body was returned to the caller, this supported direct data exfiltration rather than only blind interaction, and control over the method, headers, and body permitted state-changing requests against those internal services.

### Credit

This issue was reported by [@OracleNep](https://github.com/OracleNep).

advisories.title: Unauthenticated Data Export Disclosure via Predictable Paths
advisories.summary:
### Summary

Data exports were written to the uploads folder under a path built entirely from guessable values, so on installations with local file storage they could be downloaded through the unauthenticated download route without the signed link the export job issues.

### Details

`data-export.processor.ts`, and in the Enterprise build `interface-data-export.processor.ts`, wrote each export to `nc/uploads/data-export/` under a path made of the export date and hour, the table id, and a file name formed from the base, table and view titles (the page title for interface exports) and the export minute. The export job hands the user a signed download link that expires after three hours as the intended way to fetch the file. Unless secure attachments were enabled with `NC_SECURE_ATTACHMENTS`, `attachments.controller.ts` serves every file under `nc/uploads` on local storage through its download route without authentication, so the same export was reachable by anyone who could rebuild its path. The scheduled clean-up of export files was disabled in both job services, so exports remained on disk and reachable indefinitely.

Exports are now written under a random 48-character folder, so their paths cannot be derived from known values, and an hourly job deletes them after their download links have expired.

### Impact

No authentication is required. The attacker needs the table id and the base, table and view titles that form the path, for instance from a public shared view of the table together with the base's name, and a member must have exported that view on an installation that stores files locally without secure attachments enabled. As the rest of the path is the export's date and time, an existing export could then be located and read in full, including fields hidden from the public shared view.

### Credit

This issue was reported by [@Potatonion](https://github.com/Potatonion).

advisories.title: Database Credential Exposure via Connection Test Endpoint
advisories.summary:
### Summary

The connection-test endpoint merged caller-supplied connection fields over a stored integration's configuration, so a caller could redirect the connection attempt to a host they control while inheriting the stored database password. A workspace-ownership guard added to the same route for CVE-2026-47381 was also unreachable.

### Details

The handler in `utils.controller.ts` deep-merged the request body over `integration.getConfig()`, so `connection.host`, `port` and `user` were overridden by the caller while unstated fields, including the stored password, were inherited. Both editions behaved this way, apart from vault-backed configurations in the Enterprise edition. PostgreSQL md5 and MySQL challenge-response handshakes are offline-crackable, so a connectivity check became credential extraction, although NocoDB masks stored connection secrets on read elsewhere.

Separately, the workspace-mismatch check added by the CVE-2026-47381 fix was conditioned on a request property the extract-ids middleware never populates on this route: the ACL is declared at organization scope, and the default-workspace fallback applies only to workspace- and base-scope ACLs. The membership fallback beneath it was skipped outright for organization-level creators. The Enterprise controller overrides this method and enforces workspace membership, and the community edition has no second workspace, so the dead guard was latent. The private-integration check is unaffected by either issue.

A test that names a saved connection now takes only the database and schema from the request and refuses any other client or target field, so stored credentials only go to the stored host. The unreachable workspace check has been removed.

### Impact

A caller already authorized on an integration could point its stored credentials at a server they control and capture the database password, escalating NocoDB-mediated access into raw credentials for the connected database. The unreachable ownership guard left CVE-2026-47381 unmitigated on this route and would have failed open had the community edition gained multi-workspace support.

### Credit

This issue was reported by uu K. It was independently reported by [@sfwani](https://github.com/sfwani).

advisories.title: Metadata Database Exposure via Client-Controlled Source Flag
advisories.summary:
### Summary

The data source creation and base creation endpoints accepted the server-owned flags that mark a source as NocoDB's own database, letting a user with the Creator role attach NocoDB's internal database to their base.

### Details

Source creation in `sources.service.ts`, and base creation with inline sources in `bases.service.ts`, passed the request's `is_meta` and `is_local` flags through to `Source.createBase`, whose allow-list stored them. A source carrying these flags is treated as one of NocoDB's own: `Source.getConfig` and `getConnectionConfig` ignore the configuration supplied with it and return NocoDB's own database configuration, and `NcConnectionMgrv2` hands out the internal database connection for it. When the source was added, `populateMeta` introspected that connection and registered the tables it found, including the user, token and integration tables, as tables of the caller's base, where the ordinary table and record APIs serve them. Both endpoints now discard the two flags from the request, so only the server sets them.

### Impact

An attacker needs an account with the Creator role, on a base to add a data source or in a workspace to create a base. They could expose NocoDB's internal tables in their own base, read them, including user accounts and the token and integration tables, and change those records through the same APIs, including user roles. On the community edition, and on Enterprise installations without a separate data database, the database reached this way is the metadata database of the whole instance.

### Credit

This issue was reported by [@james-yusuke](https://github.com/james-yusuke).

advisories.title: Remote Code Execution via Formula Parsed Tree SQL Injection
advisories.summary:
### Summary

The formula query builder reused a stored, client-influenceable `parsed_tree` without revalidating it, interpolating its function name into raw SQL. On a base backed by external PostgreSQL this reached remote code execution on the database host, and on a single-container SQLite metadata install it reached instance super administrator.

### Details

The builder in `parsed-tree-builder.ts` constructs SQL for a formula column from the column's stored `parsed_tree`, writing the call-expression function name straight into a `knex.raw` fragment with no binding and no allow-list. The save-time validator that rejects unknown function names runs only when a formula is created or updated; when a stored tree is present the builder reuses it without revalidating, so an attacker able to persist a tree the validator never produced reaches the raw sink with a chosen function name. Against an external PostgreSQL source whose role may run server programs, the injected SQL could run operating-system commands on the database host. Persisting such a tree was possible because the guard meant to stop a SQLite source from opening NocoDB's own metadata file compared only normalized path strings, so a kernel-resolved alias opened the real file while comparing unequal; the attached metadata database could then be written directly, which both plants the poisoned tree and, by editing the user table, grants instance super administrator. The function names of a reused tree are now re-checked against the allow-list before the builder runs, and the path guard canonicalizes the real filesystem target before the comparison.

### Impact

An attacker needs an account with the Creator or Owner role on a base, which grants the base, source and column operations the chain uses. On a default single-container install, whose metadata lives in a SQLite file, the same primitive reads every user record, password hash, API token and stored data-source credential on the instance and rewrites the attacker's own account to super administrator, defeating the boundary between a base-scoped collaborator and instance-wide authority. Where a base is connected to an external PostgreSQL server whose role may run server programs, the injection executes operating-system commands on that database host. Managed PostgreSQL offerings that forbid program execution limit the external-source case to reading and modifying data on the connected database.

### Credit

This issue was reported by [@zenniskayy2k4](https://github.com/zenniskayy2k4).

advisories.title: Server-Side JavaScript Execution via Webhook Template Injection
advisories.summary:
### Summary

Webhook URL, header and body templates are rendered with a Handlebars helper pack whose path-resolving helpers walk attacker-supplied property paths outside the template engine's guard. The engine's string-only block on prototype access was bypassed by supplying the path as an array, letting a template reach the JavaScript function constructor and run server-side code.

### Details

`webhookHelpers.ts` compiles webhook templates with Handlebars and registers the bundled helper pack. A guard added for an earlier report rejected a prototype path such as a `constructor` chain only when the path argument was a string. Several helpers resolve their path argument with a property-walk that also accepts an array and joins it with dots, so a path supplied as an array of segments passed the string-only check and resolved to the native function constructor; other helpers in the pack then invoked the value the template had built, compiling and running attacker-supplied code in the server process. Templates are rendered before the outbound request-filtering layer, so both saved webhooks and the hook-test route reached the sink. The guard now normalizes every path argument to the segments the resolver would see, regardless of type, and refuses any helper argument or result that is or contains a function.

### Impact

An attacker needs an account with the Creator role on a base, since creating, updating and testing a webhook are restricted to that role and above. Through a crafted template the attacker could execute JavaScript in the NocoDB server process, and through it operating-system commands with the server's privileges. Short of code execution, the same primitive could read process-internal values into an outbound request sent to a destination the attacker controls.

### Credit

This issue was reported by [@seslo82](https://github.com/seslo82). It was independently reported by [@anzal1](https://github.com/anzal1) and [@thakrarsagar](https://github.com/thakrarsagar).

advisories.title: Server-Side Template Injection via Webhook Helpers
advisories.summary:
### Summary

Webhook URL, header and body templates are rendered with Handlebars, and several bundled template helpers resolved attacker-supplied property paths outside the template engine, defeating the engine's protection against prototype-chain property access.

### Details

`webhookHelpers.ts` compiles webhook templates with Handlebars and registers the `handlebars-helpers-v2` helper pack. Handlebars itself denies a template any access to non-own, prototype-chain properties such as `constructor`, `prototype` and `__proto__`; that control is what closes the classic template-to-code escalation, and it is enforced while the engine evaluates the template's own syntax tree. The `pluck`, `sortBy`, `filter` and `withSort` helpers in the bundled pack each accept a dotted property path as an argument and resolve it against the render context with `get-value`, an unguarded property-walk loop that runs as ordinary JavaScript outside the engine's evaluator. A path such as `constructor.constructor` therefore walked from the webhook's data context to the native `Function` constructor without the engine's guard ever observing the access, and the resolved value was rendered into the request NocoDB then sent to the webhook's configured destination. Other helpers in the same pack call the values they are given, so the resolved constructor could also be invoked with a string from the template, compiling and running it as JavaScript in the server process.

### Impact

An attacker could run arbitrary JavaScript in the NocoDB server process through a crafted webhook template, and through it operating-system commands with the privileges of the server. Short of code execution, the same primitive read prototype-chain-reachable internals of the server process into the outbound request, which goes to a destination the attacker chooses. Exploitation requires an authenticated account with the Creator or Owner base role, since webhook creation and update are restricted to those roles; the Editor role and below can only trigger existing webhooks.

### Credit

This issue was reported by [@iaohkut-from-NightWolf-Team](https://github.com/iaohkut-from-NightWolf-Team). It was independently reported by [@utkusen](https://github.com/utkusen).

advisories.title: Stored CSS Injection via Unescaped Mention Attribute
advisories.summary:
### Summary

User mentions in rich text and comments were written into an HTML attribute without escaping single quotes, so a user could close the attribute early and add an inline style that drew over the NocoDB interface for anyone viewing the content.

### Details

The read-only rich text renderer in `markdown.ts` turns the plain-text mention syntax into a `span` through the user-mention plugin (`tiptap-markdown/extensions/nodes/mention/user/index.ts`), which put a JSON string inside a single-quoted `data-id` attribute. JSON encoding does not escape single quotes, and for a mention whose id matches no member the email and name are taken from the stored text, so a quote in that text ended the attribute and the remainder was parsed as further attributes on the element. The output then passed through DOMPurify with its default policy, which removes event-handler attributes but keeps `style`. Because mention syntax contains no HTML tags, the server-side comment sanitizer left it unchanged, so the markup rendered from row and document comments, where mentions are enabled, as well as from rich text cells.

The mention JSON is now HTML-encoded inside a double-quoted attribute and the display name is encoded as well. Rich text and comments are also sanitized for display with a stricter profile that removes `style` attributes.

### Impact

An attacker needs an account with the Commenter role on a base to post a comment, or the Editor role to write a rich text cell. The injected style could cover or rearrange the interface for every user who later viewed that comment or cell, blocking normal use of the view and misrepresenting what it showed. No script could run.

### Credit

This issue was reported by [@manus-pi](https://github.com/manus-pi).

advisories.title: Stored HTML Injection via Rich Text Cells
advisories.summary:
### Summary

Rich text cells were rendered through DOMPurify's default policy, which keeps forms, inputs, buttons, images and inline styles, so a user who could edit records could place a page-sized overlay with a working form, or a remote image, in front of other users viewing the cell.

### Details

The read-only rich text renderer in `markdown.ts` parses cell values with markdown-it, raw HTML enabled, and sanitizes the result with DOMPurify's default policy; `TextArea.vue` renders it in the expanded record, gallery and kanban cards and shared views. Cell values are stored as written. The default policy removes scripts, event handlers and script URLs, but keeps `form`, `input`, `button` and `img` elements, `style` attributes, and `class` attributes that the application's own stylesheet can use to position an element. Stored markup could therefore draw an element over the whole interface, including a form that submits to an external address, and load images from a remote host whenever the cell was viewed. The server-side allow-list applied to comments is not applied to cell data.

Rich text is now sanitized for display with a dedicated profile: form controls other than read-only checkboxes, images, media, embeds, `style` elements and attributes, and popover attributes are removed, and only the classes and data attributes the renderer emits itself are kept.

### Impact

An attacker needs an account that can edit records in a table with a rich text field, which the Editor role grants. Every user who later viewed the cell in an expanded record, a gallery or kanban card or a shared view was shown the attacker's markup inside NocoDB, where a spoofed sign-in form could collect a password the user typed into it, and a remote image disclosed the viewer's IP address to its host. No script could run.

### Credit

This issue was reported by [@manus-pi](https://github.com/manus-pi).

advisories.title: Stored Cross-Site Scripting via Formula URL in Grid View
advisories.summary: ### Summary The canvas cell renderer used for grid views assigned the rendered output of a `URL()` formula to `innerHTML` without sanitization, so a record's text value containing markup executed script for any user who opened the table in grid mode. ### Details The link-building helper in `urlUtils.ts` handles a formula's `URI::(...)` segments: the valid-URL branch builds an anchor safely through `document.createElement` and `textContent`, but the branch for a segment whose content is not a valid URL returned the user-controlled label as raw, unencoded HTML. The canvas grid's formula cell renderer passed that string to `renderFormulaURL` in `canvas.ts`, which assigned it to `container.innerHTML` on a detached `div` used only for text measurement and link-box extraction - detached is enough for an `` or `

advisories.title: SQL Injection via Select Field Option Titles
advisories.summary:
### Summary

On MySQL and MariaDB sources, select-field option titles are embedded into `enum`/`set` column
definitions with only single-quote doubling, so a title ending in a backslash escapes the closing
quote and the attacker's remaining text is parsed as `ALTER TABLE` syntax.

### Details

The columns service builds the column's type-parameter value list by joining option titles and
replacing `'` with `''`, leaving backslashes intact. The shared validator in `sqlSanitize.ts` models
SQL string literals as quote-doubling only - correct for PostgreSQL, SQLite and SQL Server, but not
for MySQL under its default `sql_mode`, where a backslash escapes the character that follows. A
title ending in `\` therefore passes validation, and `MysqlClient.ts` interpolates the validated
value directly into the DDL statement. The CSV type detector, the Airtable import processor and the
v3 tables service build the list the same way, and it reaches the same DDL. The validator's
enum-list branch was introduced as the fix for GHSA-xj66-9p6m-wr56, so this bypasses that control
rather than describing an unrelated defect.

Backslashes inside the option literals are now doubled before the list is placed in a MySQL or
MariaDB column definition, so each option title stays inside its literal.

### Impact

A user with schema-edit rights on a base - base creator or owner - can append arbitrary clauses to
the generated `ALTER TABLE` statement on any MySQL or MariaDB source that base can write to: adding,
dropping or renaming columns, altering table options and indexes, or defining generated columns that
widen the primitive toward reading data the injection itself cannot return. The affected surface is
the connected external database, which may hold tables and columns NocoDB does not expose. Sources
running PostgreSQL or SQLite are not affected.

### Credit

This issue was reported by uu K.

advisories.title: SQL Injection via Formula Date Format Argument on MySQL
advisories.summary:
### Summary

The format argument of the `DATETIME_FORMAT` formula function was written into a MySQL string literal without escaping backslashes. A user allowed to add or edit formula fields on a MySQL-backed base could end that literal early and have the rest of the argument compiled as SQL.

### Details

On MySQL, the `DATETIME_FORMAT` mapping in `functionMappings/mysql.ts` passes the format to `datetime-format.mysql.handler.ts`, which translates it into a `DATE_FORMAT` pattern and places that pattern in the query as a quoted string inside raw SQL. `extractDatetimeFormat` in `commonFns.ts` only checks that the format is a constant string. The handler escaped `%` in literal text and doubled single quotes, but left backslashes as they were. Under MySQL's default `sql_mode` a backslash escapes the character that follows it, so a backslash placed before a quote cancelled the doubling and ended the string, and the rest of the format was compiled as part of the statement. That statement runs as the data source's database user whenever the field is evaluated, including on reads of its table. The PostgreSQL and SQLite handlers were not affected, nor were MySQL servers running with `NO_BACKSLASH_ESCAPES`. The MySQL handler now escapes backslashes in literal text before the pattern is quoted.

### Impact

An attacker needs an account that can add or edit fields on a base whose data source is MySQL or MariaDB, which the Creator role allows. They could run SQL of their choosing within the queries NocoDB issues for that base, as the data source's database user, and read any data that user can reach, including tables outside the base. Expensive queries could also slow the database server for its other users. Bases on PostgreSQL or SQLite were not affected.

### Credit

This issue was reported by [@scofaild23](https://github.com/scofaild23).

advisories.title: SQL Injection via Formula Parsed Tree Operator
advisories.summary:
### Summary

The table-creation API accepted a client-supplied formula `parsed_tree` and persisted it without rebuilding it from the formula text. At query time the stored binary-operator value was interpolated into raw SQL, so a crafted operator injected SQL against the base's data source.

### Details

Creating a table through `tables.service.ts` passes each column's properties through `getColumnPropsFromUIDT`, which spreads the caller's object and kept a supplied `parsed_tree`; `Column.bulkInsert` then persisted that syntax tree for the formula column instead of one derived from the validated formula text. When the formula was later evaluated, `parsed-tree-builder.ts` interpolated the tree's binary-expression operator into a `knex.raw` fragment without binding or validating it, whereas the save-time check only ever inspected call-expression function names. A crafted operator value therefore terminated the intended expression and appended attacker-controlled SQL, which ran against whatever database backs the base. On a single-container install whose metadata is held in the same SQLite database, this read the internal user and token tables and let the attacker's own account be rewritten to super administrator. Table creation now rebuilds the formula tree from the formula text and discards any client-supplied tree, and the operator of a reused stored tree is checked against the parser's own operator set before the builder runs.

### Impact

An attacker needs an account with the Creator role on a base, which is required to create a table or add a formula column. The injected SQL runs with the privileges of the base's data-source connection. On an install that keeps its metadata in SQLite, this exposed every user record and token on the instance and allowed the attacker to gain the super administrator role; against an external data source it allowed reading and modifying data on the connected database. No action by another user is required.

### Credit

This issue was reported by [@HDdssX](https://github.com/HDdssX).

advisories.title: SQL Injection via Zero-Argument Functions in Column Defaults
advisories.summary:
### Summary

The column default value supplied when creating or altering a column was accepted as a raw SQL expression whenever it looked like a zero-argument function call, so any such database function could be planted in a column definition and executed by the data source.

### Details

The default-value sanitiser in `KnexClient.ts` tested the submitted value against a pattern for a bare word followed by empty parentheses. A value matching that shape was emitted verbatim into the generated column definition by the PostgreSQL and MySQL data-definition emitters (`PgClient.ts`, `MysqlClient.ts`), while anything else was passed as a bound string literal. Because the check validated only the shape of the value and not the identity of the function, names such as `version()`, `current_user()`, `current_database()`, `inet_server_addr()`, `pg_postmaster_start_time()`, `txid_current()`, `pg_backend_pid()`, `pg_is_in_recovery()` and `connection_id()` reached the database unchanged. The function then ran on the database server every time a row was inserted without an explicit value for the column, and its result was stored in the row and readable through the ordinary data APIs.

### Impact

Execution of arbitrary zero-argument functions on the database behind the base, with the results returned to the attacker through normal record reads. This disclosed the database engine version, the current database and role names, internal server addresses, server start and configuration timestamps, backend process and transaction identifiers, and replica state - details that support further attacks on the data source. Exploitation requires an authenticated account with schema-edit permission on the base, that is the Creator or Owner base role; the Editor role and below cannot create or alter columns.

### Credit

This issue was reported by [@TuanHung1149](https://github.com/TuanHung1149).

advisories.title: SQL Injection via Column Precision Value
advisories.summary:
### Summary

The precision supplied when creating or updating a column was written into the generated data-definition statement without being checked, so a crafted value could append arbitrary SQL to the statement.

### Details

Column precision is placed inside the type declaration of the emitted data-definition statement. On the MySQL and SQLite clients (`MysqlClient.ts`, `SqliteClient.ts`) and in the column data backup handler, the value travelled from the request body to statement construction with no check that it was numeric, so a value that closed the type declaration turned the rest of the string into additional SQL. The PostgreSQL, SQL Server and Oracle clients were not affected, since they either omit the precision from generated statements or coerce it through integer parsing first.

### Impact

A user able to change a table's schema could execute arbitrary statements against the base's data source, including data-definition and data-manipulation statements well beyond the column change the API exposes. Exploitation requires an authenticated account with schema-edit permission on the base, that is the Creator or Owner base role; the Editor role and below cannot create or alter columns.

### Credit

This issue was reported by [@meifukun](https://github.com/meifukun).

advisories.title: Shared Base Password Disclosure via Base Metadata Endpoint
advisories.summary:
### Summary

The general base metadata endpoint returned the base record's stored password field in plaintext to any holder of a shared-base link, including callers with no account.

### Details

The dedicated shared-base metadata route was correctly limited to an id and a title, but the general base read in `bases.controller.ts` resolved on the viewer-tier role a shared-base session is granted, and nothing removed the password column from the base row before it was serialized. The sanitizer on that path, `sanitizeBase.ts`, stripped only data-source connection configuration and never touched the password field, and the controller discarded the sanitized copy it received and responded with the original object - so the sanitizer was not load-bearing for anything it did not mutate in place. The base list response carried the field as well. The value itself was vestigial: shared bases have no password feature, and the stored value was never verified against anything.

### Impact

No authentication is required beyond possession of the share link, which is precisely the artifact a shared base is handed out on. Any recipient of the link could read a stored plaintext password associated with the base; because people reuse passwords across systems, its value is not limited to the base it was set on.

### Credit

This issue was reported by [@komyunghan](https://github.com/komyunghan).

advisories.title: Hidden Column Disclosure via Shared View Group-By Column Names
advisories.summary:
### Summary

The public group-by endpoint of a shared view checked the requested column against the view's visible columns by title or id only, while the query builder also accepts a column's physical name, and it did not check the sub-group column at all. Anyone holding the share link could group by a column the owner hid from the view.

### Details

`restrictSharedViewColumnReferences` in `sharedViewQueryHelpers.ts` resolved each group-by reference through the model's titles and ids, rejected one that resolved to a hidden column, and let through any it could not resolve. The group-by builder in `BaseModelSqlv2/group-by.ts` resolves a reference by title or by physical column name, so a hidden column named by its physical name passed the check and was grouped on, returning its distinct values with their counts. The sub-group parameter was not among the checked keys; the builder resolved it the same way and returned, for each group, the number of distinct values of the named column. The group-by count builder also resolved physical names without a visibility check. Both builders now check every resolved column against the view's exposed columns and answer a hidden column the same way as an unknown one, and the service check also inspects the sub-group parameter.

### Impact

No authentication is required: the attacker needs the link to a shared view, and its password if it has one. They could read the values of columns the owner hid from that view, for the rows its filter allows, and learn which hidden columns exist and how many distinct values each holds.

### Credit

This issue was reported by [@nkedia9009-crypto](https://github.com/nkedia9009-crypto) (Naman Kedia).

advisories.title: Hidden Column Disclosure via Comma-Separated Group-By Columns
advisories.summary:
### Summary

The public group-by endpoint of a shared view checked a requested column list as a single reference, while the query builder splits it on commas. A list pairing a visible column with a hidden one passed the check and returned the hidden column's values.

### Details

`restrictSharedViewColumnReferences` in `sharedViewQueryHelpers.ts` resolved the whole group-by column value against the view's columns, rejected it only when it resolved to a hidden column, and let through any value it could not resolve. The group-by builder in `BaseModelSqlv2/group-by.ts` splits that value on commas and groups by each part, looking each one up among all of the table's columns. A comma-joined list naming a visible and a hidden column resolved to no single column, passed the check, and returned the hidden value of each group next to the visible one, which ties hidden values to individual rows when the visible column is unique. The group-by count route accepted the same list. The builders now check each part against the view's exposed columns and answer a hidden column the same way as an unknown one, and the service check validates every comma-separated part.

### Impact

No authentication is required: the attacker needs the link to a shared view, and its password if it has one. They could read the values of any column the owner hid from that view, for the rows its filter allows, paired with the values of a visible column.

### Credit

This issue was reported by [@SamCyber001](https://github.com/SamCyber001). It was independently reported by [@nkedia9009-crypto](https://github.com/nkedia9009-crypto) (Naman Kedia).

advisories.title: Missing Authorization on Job Status Polling Endpoint
advisories.summary:
### Summary

The job status polling endpoint in `jobs.controller.ts` was the only non-public job route that carried no `@Acl` decorator, so it was reachable with no credentials at all and served a background job's buffered status messages to whoever supplied the job id.

### Details

The controller's guards authenticate nothing on their own: `MetaApiLimiterGuard` only governs rate limiting, and `GlobalGuard` assigns a default guest identity when no credential validates instead of rejecting the request. The actual authentication cut-off - the `isAuthorized` check in `extract-ids.middleware.ts` - lives inside the ACL interceptor, which is mounted only by the `@Acl` decorator, so a route without one has no authentication gate whatsoever.

The handler took the job id straight from the request body and used it as the key into the polling message buffer, read from a literal `root` cache namespace shared by every tenant. The job's recorded owner (`fk_user_id`) was never consulted, and no workspace or base scope entered the lookup, so the id alone was sufficient to read the stream.

### Impact

No authentication is required, but the caller needs the job's id, an unguessable nanoid that the base's job list returns to every member of the base, including the Viewer role. With it, a caller could read that job's status updates and completion payload while the job ran and for about a minute after it ended. For a data-export job the payload carries the signed download URL of the exported file, which retrieves another user's exported data with no further authentication; for a duplication job it discloses the identifier of the new base. The impact is disclosure only.

### Credit

This issue was reported by [@Humbertosp](https://github.com/Humbertosp). It was independently reported by [@skeletonsec](https://github.com/skeletonsec) and [@klydz](https://github.com/klydz) (Adem El Adeb and Walless Al Essa).

advisories.title: Shared View Row Filter Bypass via Primary Key Lookup
advisories.summary:
### Summary

Public shared-view endpoints that resolved a record by its primary key did not apply the view's row filter, so an anonymous holder of a share link could reach records the view was configured to exclude.

### Details

A shared view's row filter is the publisher's access boundary for anonymous recipients. In `BaseModelSqlv2.ts`, the list and count paths built their WHERE clause from that filter, but the fetch-by-primary-key path constrained the query only on the key itself, row-level security, and the soft-delete flag.

Three public route families in `public-datas.service.ts` used that fetch-by-primary-key path as their record-visibility check: the many-to-many and link-to-another-record endpoints, the has-many endpoint, and the single-record read that gates the public attachment download registered in `public-datas.controller.ts`. Two of them carried a comment stating that the parent record's visibility in the shared view had been verified, an intent the call did not implement.

### Impact

No authentication is required: an attacker needs only the share link, which is meant to be distributed, plus the view password when one is configured. Because primary keys on NocoDB-created tables are sequential integers, an anonymous recipient could enumerate excluded records and read their linked-record data and download their attachment files, defeating the row filter that defines what the share exposes.

### Credit

This issue was reported by [@Pig-Tail](https://github.com/Pig-Tail), and independently by [@KasperBuilds](https://github.com/KasperBuilds), [@S2Lobby](https://github.com/S2Lobby), [@CyberKareem](https://github.com/CyberKareem), [@arpitjain099](https://github.com/arpitjain099) and [@komyunghan](https://github.com/komyunghan).

advisories.title: Shared View Attachment Disclosure via Record ID Enumeration
advisories.summary:
### Summary

The public attachment-download endpoint of a shared view resolved records by primary key through a read path that enforced the view's row filter on some database backends but not on others, exposing attachments of filtered-out records on the unenforced ones.

### Details

The single-record read in `public-datas.service.ts` scopes its base model to the shared view and then fetches the row by primary key. Which implementation served that fetch depended on the edition and the data source engine, as selected by `canUseOptimisedQuery.ts`: the optimised single-query read in `single-query-read.ts`, used for Postgres, MSSQL and Oracle on NocoDB Cloud and licensed self-hosted Enterprise, resolved the view's root filter list and applied it alongside the key predicate, whereas the fallback read in `BaseModelSqlv2.ts` - the path taken by community builds, by unlicensed self-hosted Enterprise, and by MySQL and SQLite data sources - applied only the key, row-level security and the soft-delete filter. On that path a filtered-out record resolved normally by its primary key. The same filter-blind read also backed the parent-visibility checks of the nested-link listing endpoints and the enterprise smart-text read.

### Impact

No authentication is required; the attacker holds only the public share link and, where configured, the view password. By enumerating sequential primary keys against an attachment column the view shows, an anonymous caller could obtain signed download paths for documents, images and other files attached to records the shared view was explicitly configured to exclude. Community and unlicensed self-hosted Enterprise deployments on any database, and other deployments backed by MySQL or SQLite data sources, were exposed; NocoDB Cloud and licensed self-hosted Enterprise deployments on Postgres, MSSQL or Oracle took the read path that already enforced the filter.

### Credit

This issue was reported by [@S2Lobby](https://github.com/S2Lobby).

advisories.title: Incorrect Authorization via Base Member Removal
advisories.summary:
### Summary

The check meant to stop a base member from removing someone with a higher base role never took effect, so a base Creator could remove an Owner of the base.

### Details

`baseUserDelete` in `base-users.service.ts`, in both the Community and Enterprise services, compared the target's role power with the caller's through `getProjectRolePower`, which expects a user and reads its `base_roles`. The target side was given `baseUser.base_roles`, the roles themselves, so the helper found no roles on it and returned -1, and the comparison could never refuse the request. Base Creators hold the member removal permission, so a Creator could remove a member with the higher Owner role. The separate checks that keep the last Owner of a base and protect super admins were unaffected. The target user is now passed to the comparison, so removing a member whose role outranks the caller's is refused.

### Impact

An attacker needs an account with the Creator role on the base. They could remove another Owner of the base, a role above their own, as long as at least one Owner remained. Super admins and the base's last Owner could not be removed this way.

### Credit

This issue was reported by [@sfwani](https://github.com/sfwani).

advisories.title: Incorrect Authorization via Unenforced Route Role Restrictions
advisories.summary:
### Summary

The role restriction that routes declare through the `allowedRoles` option of the `@Acl` decorator was not enforced, so access was decided by the role permission table alone. In Community Edition builds up to 0.301.3, that table let an organization Creator generate a password reset link for the super admin.

### Details

In `aclFn` (`extract-ids.middleware.ts`, Community and Enterprise), `allowedRoles` was read only inside a condition that rejects callers holding no recognised role, so it never refused a caller who held some other role, and the decision came from the role permission table. Community Edition releases from 0.202.6 to 0.301.3 granted the organization Creator role the user management permissions behind `org-users.controller.ts`, whose routes are declared for the super admin, including listing users and generating a password reset link. `generateResetUrl` in `org-users.service.ts` checked neither the caller nor the target and returned the reset token in its response. Release 0.301.4 removed those permissions from the role, and the Enterprise role table never granted them. The Enterprise table did grant the organization SSO client list to organization Creators although the route is declared for organization Owners, and the list returns each client's configuration, including its client secret. On NocoDB Cloud, workspace Creators likewise reached the workspace SSO client routes declared for workspace Owners. The middleware now refuses a caller who holds none of the declared roles.

### Impact

An attacker needs an account with the organization Creator role, or on NocoDB Cloud the workspace Creator role. On Community Edition builds from 0.202.6 to 0.301.3, an organization Creator could generate a password reset link for the super admin, set a new password and sign in as the super admin, taking control of the instance. In the Enterprise build, an organization Creator could read the organization's SSO client secrets, and on NocoDB Cloud a workspace Creator could list, add, change and delete the workspace's SSO clients.

### Credit

This issue was reported by [@123abab123789](https://github.com/123abab123789).

advisories.title: Cross-Base Authorization Bypass via MCP Token Identifier
advisories.summary:
### Summary

The request id-extraction middleware accepted an MCP token identifier from the query string on any route carrying a base id and used it to re-point the base against which the caller's roles were resolved, while the data context stayed on the base named in the path.

### Details

`extract-ids.middleware.ts` resolves two independent anchors on every request: the data anchor, which decides whose data the handler operates on, and the role anchor, which decides which base the caller's roles are resolved for. On the base-scoped branch the middleware read the MCP token id from the route parameters *or* the query string, resolved the token through the model under a full-bypass scope - so any token id on the instance resolved, unlike the service layer, which filters on the owning user - and assigned the token's base to the role anchor. The data anchor was never rewritten. No route in the tree pairs an MCP token id with a base id, so the query-string fallback had no legitimate consumer; its only effect was to let a caller pass the permission check with roles they hold on their own base while the handler served the base named in the path. The same code was present in the Community and Enterprise middleware.

### Impact

An authenticated user holding no more than the Viewer role on a single base could mint an MCP token on that base - Viewers are permitted to - and then use its id to read another base's metadata, including the table list and the base user roster with member email addresses, with no role of any kind on the target base. Writes did not follow, because the invite path re-resolves the caller's power against the data base, so the impact is cross-base read disclosure. Requires an authenticated account with at least Viewer on one unrelated base.

### Credit

This issue was reported by [@Humbertosp](https://github.com/Humbertosp).

advisories.title: Read-Only Source Restriction Bypass via Internal Batch API
advisories.summary:
### Summary

Write operations submitted through the internal batch endpoint were authorized against the source named on the outer envelope rather than the source actually targeted, letting a base Editor write to a source configured as data-read-only.

### Details

`internal.controller.ts` builds each batch sub-request with `Object.create(req)` and replaces only `query` and `body`, so authorization-relevant properties already resolved by the ID-extraction middleware - notably the source id derived from the envelope's table - were inherited by the sub-request. The dispatcher also accepted every registered operation except a nested batch, including the data-write operations, even though the SDK describes the batch set as read-only. A caller could therefore name a table from a writable source on the envelope and a table belonging to a data-read-only source inside a `dataUpdate`, `dataInsert` or `dataDelete` sub-operation: the read-only assertion in `extract-ids.middleware.ts` evaluated the writable decoy source and allowed the request, while `data-table.service.ts` resolved the inner table and performed the write without re-checking the restriction on the actual target source.

### Impact

Requires an authenticated base Editor role, or any other base role carrying data-write permission, plus knowledge of workspace, base and table identifiers that are ordinarily visible to a base member. Such a user could insert, update, move or delete records in a source the base owner had explicitly configured as data-read-only, corrupting or destroying data in an attached production database and defeating the source-level write boundary.

### Credit

This issue was reported by [@l0h1nth](https://github.com/l0h1nth).

advisories.title: Shared View Row Filter Bypass via Attachment Download
advisories.summary:
### Summary

The public attachment-download route of a shared view resolved the target record by primary key through a read that did not apply the view's row filter, so an anonymous link holder could obtain a working download link for a file attached to a record the filter excludes.

### Details

The shared-view password check in `public-datas.service.ts` was present and correct, but the record lookup performed after it went through the read-by-primary-key path in `BaseModelSqlv2.ts`, which applied only the key, row-level security and the soft-delete flag, never the view's root filter list applied by the listing path. `attachments.service.ts` then required the caller's supplied path to match a value actually stored on that record - so it was not an arbitrary-path oracle - and signed a time-limited download URL for it. Under `NC_SECURE_ATTACHMENTS=true`, where no raw path-based download route exists and previously issued signed links expire, this route was an anonymous means of minting a fresh working link to an excluded record's file. The nested-link listing endpoints, which gate on the same read, were affected by the same gap.

### Impact

No authentication is required; the share link, and the view password where one is configured, are sufficient. The relation vector needed only an enumerable record id and the id of a link column shown in the view, and returned that excluded record's linked-record data. The attachment vector additionally required the file's exact stored path, and under secure attachment storage yielded a downloadable copy of a file belonging to a record the view's filter was configured to hide.

### Credit

This issue was reported by [@komyunghan](https://github.com/komyunghan).

advisories.title: Shared View Row Filter Bypass via Linked Record Endpoints
advisories.summary:
### Summary

The public relation endpoints of a shared view checked parent-record visibility with a primary-key read that did not apply the view's row filter, letting an anonymous share-link holder read the linked records of rows the filter excludes.

### Details

The has-many, many-to-many, link-to-another-record and one-to-many routes in `public-datas.controller.ts` are served by two handlers in `public-datas.service.ts`, each of which fetched the parent row by the caller-supplied id before returning its relations. That read, in `BaseModelSqlv2.ts`, applied only the primary key, row-level security and the soft-delete filter, never the view's root filter list that the row-listing path applies - so any valid primary key satisfied the visibility gate.

The column-level hardening already present on these same handlers, namely the check that the relation column is shown in the view and the restriction applied to nested-link queries, constrains which relation column may be named rather than which parent row may be addressed, so it did not cover this case. The routes themselves carry only the public rate-limiting guard, which performs no authentication.

### Impact

No authentication is required beyond the shared-view link and its password, if one is set. Since primary keys are typically auto-increment integers, an anonymous link holder could enumerate them and read the linked and related records of rows the view's filter was meant to exclude, defeating row-level scoping of the share. Access remains confined to the shared base.

### Credit

This issue was reported by [@CyberKareem](https://github.com/CyberKareem).

advisories.title: Insecure Direct Object Reference in Shared View Record Read
advisories.summary:
### Summary

Public shared-view handlers accepted a caller-supplied primary key as a direct object reference and resolved it through a single-record read that never applied the view's row filter, making records the filter hides reachable through the share link.

### Details

In `BaseModelSqlv2.ts` the list path composed its WHERE clause from row-level security plus the view's root filter list, while the single-record read composed it from the primary-key match, row-level security, and the soft-delete flag only. In community builds row-level security resolves to an empty set, so "primary key equals the supplied id and not soft-deleted" was the complete row constraint on that path.

The public handlers in `public-datas.service.ts` that take a record id straight from the request URL - the attachment-download read and the many-to-many and has-many link listings - all resolved rows through it. For the attachment case, `attachments.service.ts` then read the attachment value out of the excluded record, matched it against the caller-supplied path, and minted a short-lived signed URL for the file.

### Impact

No authentication is required; the attacker needs the shared-view link and, if the owner set one, the share password. No public route returns a filtered-out record's scalar fields, so the disclosure was bounded by what those two handlers return: the attachment files of excluded records, and the identity of their linked records - that is, the file contents and relationship graph of records the publisher intended to withhold from the share.

### Credit

This issue was reported by [@arpitjain099](https://github.com/arpitjain099).

advisories.title: Shared View Row Filter Bypass via Row-Scoped Public APIs
advisories.summary:
### Summary

The row-scoped endpoints of a public shared view verified the target record with a primary-key read that ignored the view's row filter, while the view's own list and count endpoints enforced it. The mere existence of a primary key was enough to pass that check.

### Details

In `BaseModelSqlv2.ts` the list and count paths applied the view's root filter list whenever a view was bound to the model, while the read-by-primary-key path applied only the key predicate, row-level security, and the soft-delete filter. The row-scoped public handlers in `public-datas.service.ts` - the linked-record listings behind the many-to-many, link-to-another-record, one-to-many and has-many routes, and the single-record read behind the attachment-download route - all used that read as their "row is visible in the shared view" gate, so key existence rather than membership of the filtered set decided access. The routes in `public-datas.controller.ts` are intentionally unauthenticated, which left the row filter as their only boundary.

This is distinct from the documented behaviour whereby columns hidden in a view remain queryable; what was bypassed here is the row filter that determines which records are shared at all.

### Impact

No authentication is required beyond possession of the shared-view link and, where configured, its password. A recipient able to guess a filtered-out record's primary key - an auto-increment integer in the common case - could list that record's linked records and obtain signed download paths for its attachments, and the linked-record responses could additionally echo display fields of the excluded parent record.

### Credit

This issue was reported by [@KasperBuilds](https://github.com/KasperBuilds).

advisories.title: Account Takeover via Shared Invitation Token
advisories.summary:
### Summary

A batch invitation issued one shared invite token to every recipient, so any one invitee could complete another invitee's signup and take control of that pending account.

### Details

The organisation, base and workspace invite paths - `org-users.service.ts`, `base-users.service.ts` and `workspace-users.service.ts`, with the enterprise overrides of the latter two carrying the same shape independently - generated a single token value outside the per-recipient loop and stored it on every user row the operation created. Signup acceptance in `users.service.ts` looked the pending user up by the submitted email address and then compared the submitted token against that row's own token, so a token shared across the batch validated for every address in it; the holder could set the password on an account that was never theirs. A defective expiry check compounded this: the invite token's expiry was compared as a stored string against a `Date`, a comparison that never evaluated true, so tokens did not age out.

### Impact

A user who received one invitation could take over the pending account of any other user invited in the same operation, including an account invited at a higher role, by completing that signup and choosing its password. Exploitation requires holding a valid invitation issued in the same batch as the target.

### Credit

This issue was reported by [@aisle-research](https://github.com/aisle-research) (AISLE).

advisories.title: Cross-Base Database Access via Source Identifier Collision
advisories.summary:
### Summary

Source metadata is keyed on the pair of base id and source id, but live external-database connections were cached under the bare source id, and source creation persisted a caller-supplied id - so a source added to one base could be served another base's live connection.

### Details

`NcConnectionMgrv2.ts` stored, retrieved, evicted and version-tracked knex connections using `source.id` alone, while the sources metadata table has a composite primary key of base id and source id, so two bases may legitimately hold sources sharing an id. `Source.createBase` in `Source.ts` extracted `id` from the request body and persisted it, and both the inline sources accepted during base creation and the base-scoped add-source endpoint reach that function. A Creator on any base could therefore add a source to that base reusing a victim source's id; when the victim connection was already cached in the same process - opening a public shared view is enough to prime it - schema reflection and every subsequent record query on the attacker's source received the victim's connection, while authorization was correctly evaluated against the attacker's own base and models.
